title: Food waste in households
prompt: Households in many countries throw away large amounts of food. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to reduce it?

sentences.text: Discarded food has become a growing concern in modern societies, where supermarkets and homes alike routinely throw away edible products.
sentences.why: Neutral background that frames the issue without copying the question. Discarded food and edible products are precise paraphrases, and where supermarkets and homes alike shows range.

sentences.text: This practice damages both the environment and household finances, but it can be reduced through better planning by consumers and clearer rules for retailers.
sentences.why: A roadmap thesis that answers both questions in one sentence: the problems, then the solutions. Both and but organise the sentence, so the reader knows the plan for Coherence.

sentences.text: The most serious consequence of food waste is its contribution to environmental damage.
sentences.why: A clear topic sentence that ranks the main problem. The most serious consequence of is a strong academic phrase, and the paragraph is limited to one theme for Coherence.

sentences.text: When food decomposes in landfill sites, it releases methane, a greenhouse gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, while the water and energy used to produce the food are lost as well.
sentences.why: Explains the mechanism with a time clause and an appositive, a greenhouse gas that traps more heat. Technical vocabulary and two linked problems show Lexical Resource and development.

sentences.text: For instance, a single wasted loaf represents the wheat, fuel and transport that were needed to bake and deliver it, all of which were spent for no benefit.
sentences.why: A concrete example that makes the idea easy to picture. The list wheat, fuel and transport is parallel, and the relative clause all of which adds complex grammar accurately.

sentences.text: Waste also costs families money, because each discarded item is a purchase that provided no nourishment.
sentences.why: Adds the second problem from the thesis in one clear sentence. Because gives the reason, and the contrast between a purchase and no nourishment makes the financial loss easy to see.

sentences.text: To tackle this problem, action is needed from both individuals and retailers.
sentences.why: Moves from problems to solutions with an infinitive of purpose. Both individuals and retailers matches the thesis, so the second paragraph is clearly linked to the plan.

sentences.text: Households can reduce waste by planning meals, writing shopping lists and storing food correctly, which prevents impulse purchases and early spoilage.
sentences.why: Gives the first solution as three parallel gerunds and explains its effect with which prevents. The solution is practical and the explanation shows how it addresses the problem.

sentences.text: Supermarkets, meanwhile, could be required to donate unsold but safe products to charities, as legislation in France already requires.
sentences.why: Gives the second solution with a modal passive and supports it with a real example. Meanwhile changes the actor, and the reference to France makes the proposal credible.

sentences.text: If both measures were adopted widely, less food would reach landfill and more would feed people who need it.
sentences.why: A second conditional that predicts the outcome. It links back to the environmental and social problems and shows accurate control of if-clauses for Grammatical Range and Accuracy.

sentences.text: In summary, food waste harms the environment and wastes money, yet it can be reduced if households plan more carefully and retailers are obliged to donate surplus stock.
sentences.why: Restates the problems and solutions in new words using yet and if. It matches the thesis exactly, so the answer is consistent, and it brings in no new ideas.

sentences.text: Governments should therefore combine public information campaigns with firm legislation to make these habits the norm.
sentences.why: Ends with a recommendation that unites both solutions. Therefore signals the conclusion, and combine with firm legislation is precise vocabulary that gives a confident, formal finish.

analysis: The instruction asks two things: what problems does food waste cause, and what can be done to reduce it. Both questions need a full paragraph each.
Follow the order rule: Body 1 covers the problems, Body 2 the solutions. Do not mix them in pairs, because separate paragraphs make the structure easy for the examiner to follow.
Paraphrase: "throw away" becomes discard; "large amounts of food" becomes substantial quantities of edible products; "reduce it" becomes cut food waste or minimise it.
Choose two problems (environment and money) and two solutions (household planning and rules for retailers). Two developed ideas are better than four listed ones.
Keep solutions linked to the problems. Meal planning cuts spending, and donation rules keep surplus food out of landfill, which is where methane is released.

Turkish L1 watch: students often write "food wastes" or "a lot of foods" because Turkish treats these differently. Check: food is uncountable (food waste, much food), and a loaf or a purchase is countable.
The question does not ask for the history of food waste or for blame. Stay with problems and solutions.

plan.idea: Food waste is a growing concern. Thesis: it harms the environment and household budgets, but better planning and clearer retailer rules can reduce it.
Problems: methane from landfill and wasted resources; example of a loaf; families lose money on food they never eat.
Solutions: meal plans, shopping lists, correct storage; supermarkets required to donate unsold food, as in France; less landfill, more people fed.
Waste harms the environment and budgets but can be cut by households and retailers. Governments should combine campaigns with firm legislation.
